agent_notes: עֵקֶב is 'heel' as well as 'consequence, reward'. Rashi takes it as 'heel' (measure for measure, the path they walked against me); Radak, Metzudat David and Ibn Ezra take it as 'reward, recompense'. I kept 'on the heel of their shame' in the literal layer to hold both and gave the dramatic layer the sense of consequence.
Rashi's closing remark that every 'poor and needy' in the Psalms stands for Israel is a collective reading I did not carry into the commentary.

יַחֲשָׁב לִי is difficult and the five English versions split: KJV/ASV 'thinketh upon me', YLT 'doth devise for me', BBE 'has me in mind'. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David read it as 'may he reckon/credit (my humility) to me' or 'may he count me worthy'. I read it as a jussive, 'may the Lord reckon [it] to me', and kept the object open in the literal layer; the dramatic layer follows the sense 'take account of me'. The form is imperfect, not participle, so KJV's present-tense 'thinketh' is an assertion the verb does not make.
STEPBible's entity tag for אֱלֹהַי is deity.yhwh; I treated it as the vocative 'my God' and did not alter the tag.

The infinitive absolute qavveh qiviti is rendered 'waiting, I waited'. KJV/ASV 'patiently' and YLT 'diligently' add an adverb the Hebrew does not have; the root qvh also means to be stretched, twisted like a cord toward something, which I mention only as a general lexical point.

agent_notes: 'ears you dug for me': kara 'to dig' is the standard sense (cf. Ex 21:33, cited by Radak and Metzudat Zion), so 'opened' (KJV, ASV, Webster) is an interpretation, and BBE/YLT 'made/prepared' are another. The Greek of Hebrews 10:5 reads 'a body you prepared'; I do not treat this as a Hebrew variant, only mention the fact. Interpretations of the line (Sinai, obedience over sacrifice, 1 Sam 15:22) are listed from Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak.

Meaning of 'in the scroll of the book it is written of me' is disputed among the commentators: Torah of Moses (Rashi, Radak, Meiri), a vow written down in distress (Ibn Ezra), or the law written on the heart (Malbim). The literal layer keeps 'on me' (alay), which can also mean 'for me / about me / upon me as an obligation'; the dramatic layer chooses 'about me', which the commentators share.

me'ai is the bowels or inner organs, not the heart as in KJV. Radak, Rashi and Metzudat David all explain it as the inward self, with Radak noting that the heart is included among the me'im. I keep the bodily word in the literal layer and explain in the commentary.
